question: Za soumraku vypadají červené vlčí máky skoro černé, zatímco modré a zelené věci jsou ještě dobře vidět. Tento jev objevil a popsal slavný český fyziolog. Jak se jmenoval?
source_excerpt: Purkyně noticed that red flowers looked bright carmine during sunny days but appeared to change to a deep muted hue come nighttime.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has seen red flowers turn almost black at dusk without wondering why. Czech players know Purkyně's name from streets and schools but have no idea that this everyday twilight effect is named after him.
extra.verification_notes: The Purkinje effect, in which red looks dark and blue/green stay visible at dusk, was described by Jan Evangelista Purkyně in 1819 (per the search results; the sources are secondary).

explanation: Při šeru přebírají vidění tyčinky a ty jsou nejcitlivější na modrozelené světlo, ne na červené. Celý svět tomu dodnes říká Purkyňův jev.

question: Po mátové žvýkačce vám obyčejná voda z kohoutku připadá ledová, i když teplota v ústech se vůbec nezměnila. Která látka z máty takhle oklame nervy, které hlásí chlad?
source_excerpt: Menthol also opens TRPM8, and thus activates the same sensory neurons as cold, leading to the well-known cool sensation even if temperature does not change.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has felt water turn freezing after a mint gum and assumed the mint 'cools' the mouth. In fact nothing gets colder: a single chemical tricks the nerves into sending a false cold signal. Players can reason their way to the answer from the word 'mint'.
extra.verification_notes: Menthol activates the TRPM8 cold receptor, producing a cooling sensation without any temperature change; no newer finding contradicts this (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3224875).

explanation: Mentol spouští stejné receptory jako skutečný chlad, takže mozek dostane falešné hlášení 'zima'. Voda pak tento pocit ještě zesílí.
